source.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
source.authors: Alex Cloud; Minh Le; James Chua; Jan Betley; Anna Sztyber-Betley; Jacob Hilton; Samuel Marks; Owain Evans

page_placements.theme: Prompt-only and in-context analogues beyond linked tokens

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The original study applies the teacher-output filtering and student fine-tuning procedure and measures trait transmission, including same- versus different-initialization comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports classifier-detection and capability results; these are not included as rows unless they measure a claim version. Secondary storytelling and multiple-choice animal evaluations, MMLU results, and some follow-up animal experiments are not included below. In-context learning is recorded for the prompt-only analogue. Figure-only values are not estimated.
record.test_reason: This is the original source (arXiv:2507.14805). It runs the teacher, filter and student fine-tuning procedure and measures trait transmission (A, C), same- versus different-base transfer (B), mechanism probes (D), and evaluation-prompt variants (E). No verdict labels are given because the study is the claim's original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that teacher outputs carry hidden, model-specific signals that transmit traits, including misalignment, through filtered unrelated data to students sharing a similar initialization. They frame subliminal learning as a general neural-network property, supported by the theorem and the MNIST experiment, and warn that filtering may not prevent it. They acknowledge the tasks are artificial and that the conditions for transmission remain open.
record.recipe_differences: This is the original study and method: trait-bearing teachers generate filtered unrelated outputs, which are used to fine-tune students; evaluations measure the teacher trait. The study includes number, code, CoT, cross-model, ICL, and MNIST experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Transmission differs by teacher/student model type and initialization; some animals transmit for some models but not others. Number shuffling within or across responses sharply reduces animal transmission. Evaluation suffixes that make the evaluation context more like training increase effect sizes. The Qwen2.5-7B animal results are more consistent when evaluation prompts include number-sequence prefixes.

fits_no_version.finding: In-context presentation of up to the entire animal-number dataset (10K examples) gives no significant shift in GPT-4.1 nano animal preference versus regular numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transmission requires gradient updates; in-context exposure to the same teacher data does not shift the trait.

record.problems: Several outcome values are supplied only in plots. Animal transmission depends on selected animals and evaluation context; authors report some animals do not transmit in some models. The misalignment CoT filter has limited discrimination (AUC 0.620; threshold 78 yields false positive rate 37.3%). Experiments use artificial prompts and training setups; authors state practical transmission conditions remain open.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted secondary favorite-animal/tree evaluations in stories and multiple-choice formats (Appendix A, Figure 12), MMLU capability figures (Appendix A, Figure 11), animal follow-ups including the 15-animal set and finetuned teachers (Appendix B, Figures 14–15), individual Qwen animal outcomes and prompt-prefix conditions (Appendix B.2, Figure 17), and the ICL figure’s separate animal/example-count values (Figure 9). The cross-model GPT-4.1 nano/Qwen2.5-7B matrix cell values were not extracted because the flattened figure text does not unambiguously associate every value with a pair. These omissions do not exceed the row limit.

untested.parts: Traits beyond animal/tree preference and emergent misalignment; data domains beyond numbers, code and GSM8K CoT.
How similar initializations must be. Base-model mismatch is tested only among OpenAI GPT-4.x models and GPT-4.1 nano/Qwen2.5-7B.
Token entanglement, divergence tokens and steering-vector-like directions. Only the gradient theorem, number shuffling and MNIST auxiliary-logit distillation are examined.
Full fine-tuning versus LoRA, and LoRA rank. Training uses the OpenAI API with unspecified adapter settings.
Inserting selected linked tokens into a prompt without fine-tuning (subliminal prompting) is not tested.

missing.what: MNIST MLP experiment: a student distilled on teacher auxiliary logits from noise images reaches over 50% test accuracy with shared initialization. It fails with a different initialization.
Evaluation suffix resembling the training format increases effect sizes for misalignment (numbers and CoT) evaluations.
missing.locator: Appendix D.2 and D.4 evaluation suffix; Figure 4b caption

missing.what: Storytelling and multiple-choice evaluations show less consistent transmission than the favorite-animal prompt (declared left out, but bears on E's evaluation-prompt part).
Same-type cells of the GPT-4.1 nano/Qwen2.5-7B matrix (apparently 0.39* and 0.11*), plus Qwen per-animal results showing transmission only for a subset of animals without the number prefix.
missing.locator: Figure 8 right panel; Appendix B.2, Figure 17

record.verdict_notes: Original source: verdicts withheld per rules. Rows r1–r10 and r12–r20 link to E only for the train/eval prompt mismatch. For B rows, state codes whether transmission occurred. Significant small cross-model transfer (r33, r34: 0.06*, 0.07*) is partial against the strict 'fails' wording. GPT-4.1↔GPT-4o transfer (r35, r44) is attributed by the authors to a shared initialization. The CoT filter is weak (AUC 0.620), which bears on how strongly 'filtered' holds for r28.

versions.untested_parts: Tests animal/tree preferences via numbers and code, and misalignment via numbers and CoT; does not test every possible trait or unrelated-data domain.
Tests animal transmission across selected model types/initializations; does not establish a general threshold for how similar initializations must be.
Tests misalignment transfer through numbers and CoT, including false-answer outcomes on TruthfulQA; does not test every alignment-relevant trait.
Presents a gradient-descent theorem and a number-shuffling experiment; does not identify a specific token-level carrier or establish a single empirical mechanism for all settings.
Evaluates animal preference with prompts distinct from training prompts and reports that an evaluation suffix increases effects; does not compare full fine-tuning with LoRA or test other LoRA ranks.
Tests in-context examples from the training data without fine-tuning; does not test inserting only a selected linked token set into a prompt.
